title: How Ironman Triathlons Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Ironman triathlon: the race format (2.4-mile swim, 112-mile bike, marathon run), its 1978 origin in Hawaii conceived by John Collins, early media coverage via ABC's Wide World of Sports and Sports Illustrated, Julie Moss's 1982 collapse-and-crawl finish, the Kona World Championship, the discontinued lottery and Legacy slot program, the physiology of collapsing near the finish (overheating and brain shutdown theory from Brent Ruby), the post-Ironman blues, endurance-related health risks, triathlon training advice, notable athletes like James Lawrence (Iron Cowboy) and Team Hoyt, and comparisons of marathon versus Ironman difficulty. The episode closes with a listener mail from Betty about Louisiana Cajun interpreters in WWII and the Battle of Savo Sound.

segments.title: Opening banter and Seattle show announcement
segments.summary: Josh announces upcoming Seattle live show at The Moore Theatre in January and ticket sale details. Hosts joke about negative iTunes reviews calling them boring and stupid, and about digressive episodes.

segments.title: What an Ironman race is and the name
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Ironman distances: 2.4-mile swim, 112-mile bike, and full marathon run, held at the World Championship in Kona, Hawaii. They note the term is gender neutral and discuss the plural forms of Ironman.

segments.title: Origins of triathlon and the first Ironman
segments.summary: Triathlon origins in San Diego in 1974 and Navy officer John Collins bringing the idea to Hawaii. The first Ironman combined existing Hawaii endurance events, and twelve finishers were named Ironmen. Early race logistics and a dispute over organizer liability and ownership are described.

segments.title: Media coverage and Julie Moss's finish
segments.summary: ABC's Wide World of Sports and Sports Illustrated helped popularize Ironman. Julie Moss collapsed and crawled to second place in the fourth Ironman, while Kathleen McCartney won. Participation grew rapidly afterward.

segments.title: Why endurance athletes collapse near the finish
segments.summary: Discussion of theories for collapsing before the finish line: fuel depletion, lactic acid, and overheating. Physiologist Brent Ruby argues overheating and brain-driven shutdown are the main cause, and the hosts speculate about psychological triggers. They also mention the post-Ironman blues.

segments.title: Ironman qualifying, lottery and Legacy slots
segments.summary: Qualifying for Kona requires finishing other sanctioned Ironman races. The lottery that gave about five hundred slots for a fee was ended after the federal government deemed it illegal gambling, and was replaced by the Legacy program.

segments.title: Ironman race legs, transition, and cutoffs
segments.summary: Details of the swim start staggering and the wetsuit rule, transition areas where athletes change for the bike and run, the bike course winds and lava fields at Kona, the 17-hour cutoff, and the midnight finish tradition.

segments.title: Prize money, sponsorships and notable athletes
segments.summary: Prize purses at the World Championship and how elite triathletes earn money through winnings and sponsorships. Mentions of Jan Frodeno, Javier Gomez, James Lawrence the Iron Cowboy who did fifty Ironmans in fifty days, and drafting disqualification of Patricia Puntous in 1986.

segments.title: Training for a triathlon and health risks
segments.summary: Advice from articles on training for an Ironman: take a year, build endurance, rest, train to weaknesses, use race equipment, and consult a doctor. Studies linking endurance sports to atrial fibrillation and pancreatic cancer risk are discussed, along with ultra-marathon and doubling feats.

segments.title: Inspiring athletes, Team Hoyt, and Olympic and sprint comparisons
segments.summary: Stories of Team Hoyt (Dick and Rick Hoyt), Kyle and Brent Pavone, Mark Herman, Sister Madonna Buder, Jim Ward, Chris Lieto's emergency surgery, and crawling finishers. The hosts compare Olympic and sprint triathlon distances to the full Ironman and settle the marathon vs Ironman debate using average finishing times.

segments.title: Listener mail from Betty on Cajun interpreters and Savo Sound
segments.summary: Listener Betty suggests Louisiana Cajun interpreters in WWII as a parallel to the Navajo code talkers and asks about the Battle of Savo Sound. Hosts say they will look into it for a short stuff.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to the website and social links for suggestions.
